title: Drink
translation: There's a lot in this world I don't understand. Whenever there's company, the first thing people do is press drinks on each other, and they think it's fun to make someone drink when he doesn't want to. Why? I don't get it.

Look at the man doing the drinking. He frowns as if he can hardly stand it. He waits until nobody's looking to tip it away. He tries to slip out. And they grab him, drag him back and make him drink anyway, for no reason at all. A dignified man turns into a raving idiot in no time. A perfectly healthy one turns into a seriously sick man right in front of you and collapses, out cold. On a day that's meant to be a celebration, it's appalling. The next day his head still aches. He can't eat, he lies there groaning, and yesterday is gone, as if he'd been born again since. He lets important things slide, at work and at home, and it causes real trouble.

Doing that to someone is cruel, and it's rude. Anyone who's been through it must feel bitter and hard done by. If we heard that some foreign country had a custom like this, something we didn't do here, we'd think it was bizarre.

Even watching it happen to other people is miserable. Take someone you'd always found thoughtful and rather refined. Now he laughs and shouts with no restraint at all, talks far too much, his cap goes crooked, his collar comes undone, he hitches his robes up high on his legs, and he doesn't care how he looks. You'd never think it was the same man. The women push their hair back off their faces, not a bit shy, tip their heads up and laugh, and hang on to the hand that holds the cup. The coarser ones pick up bits of food and shove them into other people's mouths, and eat some themselves. It's ugly.

Everyone sings and dances at the top of their voices. Someone calls up an old priest, who bares his dark, grubby shoulders and twists about in a dance you can't bear to watch, and the people enjoying it are just as hateful. One man tells you how wonderful he is until you're embarrassed for him. Another cries into his cup. The servants swear at each other and start fighting. It's all shocking, frightening, shameful and sad. In the end they grab things they have no business touching, fall off the veranda, fall off horses and out of carriages, and hurt themselves. The ones on foot stagger down the main street and do unspeakable things against the walls and in the gateways. An old priest in his robes leans on a little boy's shoulder and lurches along, babbling things that don't bear repeating. It's painful to see.

If all this did you some good, in this life or the next, fine, there'd be nothing to say. But in this life it makes you do stupid things, it costs you money and it makes you ill. People call it the best of all medicines, but every illness starts with drink. They say it makes you forget your troubles, but look at a drunk: he's the one crying over troubles that were over long ago. And the next life? It takes away your judgement, burns up the good you've done like fire, piles on the bad, makes you break every precept, and you go to hell. The Buddha himself taught that if you pour a drink and make someone else drink it, you'll be born without hands for five hundred lives.
That's how much I dislike it. And yet, now and then, there are times you wouldn't want to do without it.

A moonlit night, a snowy morning, or out under the cherry blossoms: you're talking at your ease, someone brings out the cups, and it makes everything better. On a dull day a friend drops in out of nowhere, and you have a drink together. That's a comfort. At some grand house where you're not on familiar terms, fruit and wine are passed out to you from behind the blinds, and it's done beautifully. Very nice. In winter, in a cramped little room, you roast something over the fire, sit across from a close friend and drink a lot. That's lovely. On a journey, at some shelter or out in the hills, someone says, "What have we got to go with it?" and you drink sitting on the grass. That's fun too.

Someone who really can't drink is pressed into having a little. That's sweet. Someone grand singles you out: "Have another. You've hardly had any." You're pleased. Someone you've wanted to get to know turns out to like a drink, and you're friends in no time. You're pleased about that too.

All the same, drinkers are funny, and you forgive them. One of them, worn out from the night before, is sleeping late when the host slides the door open. He panics. Still dazed, no cap on, his thin little topknot showing, he scoops up his clothes without stopping to put them on and runs for it, dragging them behind him, the way drinkers do. All you see is his back, his robes hitched up, and a pair of skinny, hairy shins.

literal: In the world there are many things I do not understand.
Whenever there are friends, first offering sake and making it the fun to force (people) to drink: I do not understand for what reason.

The drinker's face frowns as if it were very hard to bear; he watches for when people are not looking to throw it away, tries to escape; when (they) catch him, hold him back and make him drink for no reason,
even a proper person at once becomes a madman and is ridiculous, and even a healthy person becomes, before one's eyes, a gravely sick man and collapses, knowing neither before nor after.
On days that are to be celebrated and the like, it must be appalling.

Until the next day his head aches, he lies groaning without eating, as if separated by a rebirth, does not remember yesterday's things, neglects important matters public and private, and it becomes a trouble.
To make a person go through such a thing has no compassion and goes against propriety too.
Would a person who has gone through such a bitter thing not think it hateful and regrettable?
If one heard, as the affair of others not found here, that in another country there is such a custom, it would surely seem strange and mysterious.
Even seeing it happen to other people is distressing.

Even a person whom I had seen as thoughtful-looking and admirable laughs and shouts without restraint, (uses) many words, cap askew, cords undone, shins lifted high, with a careless air: he does not seem the person of ordinary days.

The women push back their forelocks openly, unabashed, lift their faces and laugh, cling to the hand holding the cup; and vulgar people take snacks and put them to (others') mouths, and eat themselves too: an ugly sight.

Putting out their voices to the limit, each sings and dances, and an old priest is called out, bares his dark, dirty body from the shoulders, and twists so one cannot bear to look; even the people who watch with enjoyment are repellent and hateful.

Or again (one) tells of the splendid things about himself, painfully for those nearby, or (one) weeps drunk, and the lower people curse each other and quarrel, and there is nothing but appalling, frightening, shameful and wretched things,
and in the end they snatch things not permitted, fall from the veranda, fall from horses and carriages, and hurt themselves.
Those of a rank that do not ride anything stagger along the avenue, and facing earthen walls, the foot of gates and the like, do unspeakable things all over,
and an old priest wearing a surplice, holding on to the shoulder of a little boy, staggering while saying incomprehensible things: very painful to see.
If, even doing such things, it were an act that would bring benefit in this world and the next, what could one do?
In this world there are many mistakes, one loses wealth, and one gets sick.
Though it is called the chief of a hundred medicines, all illnesses arise from sake.
Though it is said to make one forget sorrow, it is the drunk person, it seems, who recalls even past griefs and weeps.
As for the next world, it makes a person lose wisdom, burns good roots like fire, increases evil, breaks all the precepts, and (he) will surely fall into hell.
'A person who takes up sake and makes others drink will be born without hands for five hundred lives': so the Buddha taught, it is said.
Though it is a thing I think so repellent, there must naturally also be times when it is hard to give up.
On moonlit nights, snowy mornings, under the blossoms too, talking with an easy heart and bringing out cups is a thing that adds to every pleasure.
On a dull day, when a friend comes in unexpectedly and (drink) is served, that too comforts the heart.
From inside the blinds of a place one is not familiar with, fruit, sake and the like being put out with a fine air: very good.
In winter, in a narrow place, roasting things on the fire and such, intimate friends facing each other and drinking a lot: very delightful.
At a traveller's shelter, in fields and hills and the like, saying 'What is there to go with it?' and drinking on the grass is also delightful.
A person who suffers badly (from drink), pressed and drinking a little, is also very good.
A person of quality, singling one out, saying things like 'One more; the top is low', is also gladdening.
That a person one wished to get close to is a drinker and one quickly becomes intimate is also gladdening.
That said, a drinker is amusing, and his faults are forgiven.

When, at the place where he slept late tired out from drinking, the master slid (the door) open, flustered, with a dazed face, sticking out his thin topknot, holding his clothes without time to put them on,
the back view of his hitched-up figure dragging (them) as he flees, his hairy thin shins: amusing and fitting.

notes.quote: 強ひ飲ませたるを興とする事
notes.text: {強|し}ふ: 'to force, to press'. Pressing drinks on guests was part of being a good host. Section 1 ends on the same custom from the other side: a man should decline at first, but he should be able to drink.

notes.quote: 生を隔てたるやうにして
notes.text: 'As if separated by a life'. The 1925 edition explains it with the Buddhist idea that you forget your previous life when you are reborn. The hangover is a small rebirth: yesterday is gone.

notes.quote: 他の国にかかる習ひあなり
notes.text: あなり: あるなり, said あんなり, with the ん not written. なり after the verb here means 'I hear, they say'. {人事|ひとごと}: 'someone else's affair'. The same kanji are read じんじ in section 174.

{烏帽子|ゑばうし}: the tall black cap that adult men wore all the time, indoors and out. Being seen bareheaded was embarrassing. That is why the drinker at the end of the section, caught without his cap, shows his thin topknot ({髻|もとどり}).

notes.quote: 額髪はれらかに掻きやり
notes.text: {額髪|ひたひがみ}: the hair that hung at the sides of a woman's face. Women of the court kept their faces half hidden; pushing the hair back and lifting the face was bold. The 1925 edition glosses はれらかに as 'openly, exposed'.
すぢる: 'to twist the body', here in a dance. The edition glosses it that way. {肩|かた}ぬぐ: to slip the robe off one's shoulders.
えもいはぬ: 'indescribable'. It often praises something as too fine for words; here it is the opposite. The 1925 edition says plainly that it means vomiting and urinating.
{聞|きこ}えぬ: 'not understandable', or 'not fit to be heard'. The 1925 edition takes it as obscene talk to the boy. The translation keeps it open.
A false friend: かはゆし means 'painful to see, pitiful'. Modern かわいい 'cute' comes from this word, but the meaning has moved a long way.
'The chief of a hundred medicines': from the Han shu, the history of the Han dynasty, which the 1925 edition cites. In Japan it became a proverb, still used today: {酒|さけ}は{百薬|ひやくやく}の{長|ちやう}.
Also from the Han shu, in the biography of Dongfang Shuo: 'nothing dispels sorrow like wine', as the edition notes. Kenkō answers both sayings with what drunk people actually do.

notes.quote: 五百生が間手なき者に生る
notes.text: The 1925 edition gives the source: the Brahma Net Sutra, which says that whoever hands a cup of wine to someone else will have no hands for five hundred lives, 'so how much worse to drink oneself'. Not drinking is one of the five basic precepts for Buddhists.

notes.quote: かく疎ましと思ふものなれど
notes.text: Here the section turns. The list of horrors becomes a list of pleasures, in the same form: a short scene, then a short verdict (いとよし, をかし, {嬉|うれ}し).
A short phrase whose exact sense is not certain. It is usually taken as a friendly push: the level in your cup has hardly gone down, so 'you've hardly drunk anything'. The translation follows that.
{上戸|じやうご}: someone who can drink, the opposite of {下戸|げこ} (section 1). Both words are still in use.
